Abstract 16

Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) is a multi-drug resistant pathogen increasingly responsible for 17

severe pulmonary infections. Analysis of whole genome sequences (WGS) of Mab demonstrates 18

dense genetic clustering of clinical isolates collected from disparate geographic locations. This 19

has been interpreted as supporting patient-to-patient transmission, but epidemiological studies 20

have contradicted this interpretation. Here we present evidence for a slowing of the Mab 21

molecular clock rate coincident with the emergence of phylogenetic clusters. We find that 22

clustered isolates are enriched in mutations affecting DNA repair machinery and have lower 23

spontaneous mutation rates in vitro. We propose that Mab adaptation to the host environment 24

through variation in DNA repair genes affects the organism’s mutation rate and that this manifests 25


<!-- Page 3 -->


2

as phylogenetic clustering. These results inform our understanding of niche switching for 26

facultative pathogens, and challenge the model of transmission as the major mode of 27

dissemination of clinically dominant Mab clusters. 28

29

Introduction 30

Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) is an emerging, multi-drug resistant pathogen that is 31

increasingly responsible for opportunistic pulmonary disease, most commonly in patients with 32

underlying structural lung conditions such as cystic fibrosis (CF)1. Mab is divided into three 33

subspecies: M. a. abscessus, M. a. massiliense, and M. a. bolletii, the former two being the most 34

clinically relevant subspecies2. Infections with Mab are associated with accelerated decline in lung 35

function and can result in severe disseminated disease and/or loss of eligibility for lung 36

transplantation. Mab infections are difficult to treat, requiring a prolonged antibiotic regimen with 37

high rates of treatment failure3. 38

Until recently, Mab infections were thought to be acquired independently by each patient 39

from environmental reservoirs in soil or water. Large scale analyses of whole genome sequencing 40

(WGS) of Mab clinical isolates have revealed that a large proportion of clinical isolates fall into 41

several phylogenetically characterized clusters, often termed dominant circulating clones4. 42

Isolates within these clusters have high core genome similarity that is not explained by point 43

source outbreaks as they were sampled from diverse geographic origins. These observations 44

have been interpreted as supporting widespread recent transmission, either through direct contact 45

or indirectly through fomites, but a number of epidemiological studies have refuted person-to- 46

person transmission as a major mode of Mab dissemination5–11. Reconciling these conflicting lines 47

of evidence is important as they dictate public health practice and allocation of resources to 48

protect vulnerable populations from infection. However, it is still unclear what role transmission 49

plays in the emergence of Mab clusters. 50


<!-- Page 4 -->


3

While widespread transmission is one proposed explanation for the phylogenetic structure 51

observed in Mab, it is important to consider other factors in the species’ evolutionary history that 52

may contribute. For example, ecological niche switching from environmental sources to a human 53

host may introduce bottlenecks resulting in low diversity and effective population size. Another 54

explanation is a change in mutation rates, either through changes in bacterial generation time or 55

through adaptive genetic variation. A third consideration is sampling bias, where particular Mab 56

lineages that cause more frequent, severe and/or persistent disease are more likely to be isolated 57

and sequenced. Consistent with the latter hypothesis, previous work has shown that isolates 58

within clusters are more likely to contain point mutations associated with antibiotic resistance and 59

are associated with greater bacterial burden and lung inflammation in mice4. 60

Interpreting tree structures in the context of population history is aided by phylogenetic 61

dating, which translates genetic distances into time scale. Previous studies4,9,12,13  have estimated 62

molecular clock rates in Mab but these have been limited to subpopulations within clusters. Here 63

we report on molecular clock rate estimation for the deep branches of the M. a. abscessus 64

phylogeny and for within-host isolates belonging to clusters. We provide evidence for an 65

evolutionary slow-down coincident with the expansion of clinically dominant clusters and propose 66

that the emergence of dense phylogenetic clustering in Mab may result from genetically encoded 67

changes to the mutation rate. These results indicate that transmission is not the only plausible 68

explanation for the dense clustering observed in the Mab phylogeny, and that more research is 69

needed to clarify the transmission dynamics of this emerging pathogen. 70

71

Results 72

Phylogenetic analysis confirms the presence of large, dominant clusters (DCs) spanning multiple 73

geographies. We identified 1,629 M. abscessus isolates with publicly available whole genome 74

sequencing (WGS) data and associated dates of collection (Extended Data Table 1). We 75


<!-- Page 5 -->


4

excluded isolates with likely contamination or low-quality assemblies (Methods). Among the 1,461 76

isolates passing quality filters, the majority (80.1%) were derived from in vitro culture of pulmonary 77

samples. Of the 1,181 pulmonary isolates, 98.3% (1,161/1,181) were collected from patients with 78

cystic fibrosis (CF), while the rest were collected from patients with no documented diagnosis. 79

The dataset represented 483 patients with unique patient identifiers, with 59.6% (288/483) of 80

patients contributing a single isolate, and the remaining contributing between 2 to 24 isolates 81

sampled over time. Isolates originated from nine countries and were collected between 1998- 82

2017, with the exception of the reference strain ATCC 19977 which was collected in 1957 (Figure 83

1B). 84

The majority (91.7%) of samples had ≥98% average nucleotide identity (ANI) with one of 85

three reference genomes (Supplementary Table 1) representing each of the three Mab 86

subspecies, consistent with the commonly used ANI threshold for bacterial subspecies. Isolates 87

with <98% ANI with any subspecies were excluded from downstream analysis. The resulting 88

dataset overrepresented clinically relevant subspecies of M. abscessus, with 93.9% belonging to 89

either M. a. abscessus or M. a. massiliense. To better resolve true evolutionary relationships 90

among samples, we defined and restricted analysis to the core genome for each subspecies, then 91

further excluded predicted recombination events (Methods). We performed maximum likelihood 92

(ML) phylogenetic analysis for each of the three Mab subspecies, using only the first isolate from 93

each patient to focus on between-host diversity. The resulting subspecies trees confirmed the 94

presence of multiple, globally distributed clades with dense phylogenetic clustering (Methods). 95

We excluded clustering due to potential point source outbreaks by limiting to clusters containing 96

isolates from more than one country and a minimum of three isolates for downstream analysis. In 97

total, we confirmed 16 clusters (Extended Data Figure 1A) including four clusters with > 50 98

isolates, which we refer to here as dominant clusters (DCs). Isolates within clusters comprised 99

76.4% of isolates included in the phylogenetic analysis. The median pairwise distance in M. a. 100


<!-- Page 6 -->


5

abscessus DC 1 was 68 SNPs. For comparison, the mean pairwise distance across the 101

subspecies trees were 5537, 4100, and 8034 SNPs for M. a. abscessus, M. a. massiliense, and 102

M. a. bolletii, respectively. All four DCs contained isolates originating from three continents (North 103

America, Europe, and Australia). Clustered isolates also spanned the full range of isolation times, 104

including ATCC 19977, which was placed within M. a. abscessus DC 1 despite having been 105

collected at least 40 years before any other isolates in the tree (Figure 1A-B). 106

107

Coalescent analysis reveals a faster long-term evolutionary rate than observed in DCs. To aid in 108

transmission inference and to reconstruct the evolutionary history of Mab, we performed a 109

coalescent analysis using our SNP alignment. Previous work has reported molecular clock rates 110

within Mab clusters, but to our knowledge no study has successfully dated any of the full Mab 111

subspecies phylogenies. To evaluate the presence of temporal signal, we performed root-to-tip 112

regression for each subspecies tree but in each case did not observe a positive correlation 113

between sampling date and root-to-tip distance. We reasoned that the high degree of population 114

structure in the Mab phylogeny may obscure the genetic-temporal signal. To test this hypothesis, 115

we pruned each subspecies tree until it contained the minimal number of samples required to 116

capture 95% of the genetic diversity in the original tree (Methods). Following pruning of the M. a. 117

abscessus subspecies tree, root-to-tip regression demonstrated the presence of temporal signal 118

(Figure 1C, D). Evidence of temporal signal in M. a. abscessus was further strengthened using a 119

permutation test and a Bayesian evaluation of temporal signal (Extended Data Figure 1C, 120

Extended Data Table 3). 121

We used a Bayesian implementation of coalescent analysis, BEAST14, to estimate the 122

molecular clock rate of the pruned M. a. abscessus subspecies tree assuming a relaxed clock 123

model, which allows each branch of the tree to have its own clock rate. To explore the effect of 124

the tree prior on molecular clock estimation, we ran analyses using two different tree priors, 125

assuming either a constant coalescent model, which assumes constant population size over time, 126


<!-- Page 7 -->


6

or a Bayesian skyline coalescent model, which allows the population size to change over time. 127

While the Bayesian skyline coalescent had a slightly better marginal likelihood, we found no 128

significant difference between the clock rates estimated by the two models (Table 1, Figure 2C). 129

Our estimates for the clock rate in the long, internal branches of the tree were approximately 10- 130

fold faster than nearly all previously reported estimates of the clock rate within Mab clusters 131

(Figure 2C). We next attempted to date the full (unpruned) M. a. abscessus phylogeny using the 132

faster rate inferred from our coalescent analysis of the pruned tree. These chains suffered from 133

poor convergence and sampled trees with a distorted topology, elongating the short branches 134

and eliminating the densely clustered structure observed in the ML phylogeny (data not shown). 135

We therefore hypothesized that the lack of temporal signal in the full M. a. abscessus dataset 136

may result from a difference between the long-term clock rate and the more recent evolutionary 137

rate within phylogenetic clusters. 138

139

Analysis of longitudinally sampled within-host isolates supports a slower clock rate in DCs. To 140

further investigate the differences in clock rate between long-term historical time scales and short- 141

term contemporary time, we used pairs of isolates sampled from the same patient over time to 142

estimate the mutation rate. We focused on estimating a within-host clock rate for M. a. abscessus 143

to compare directly with the estimate from our coalescent analysis and because we had the most 144

longitudinal samples for this subspecies. Because polyclonal Mab infection is common in CF 145

patients, we first excluded any isolate pairs with a SNP distance > 20. This threshold was selected 146

by comparing the distribution of all possible within-host isolate pairs to the distribution of pairwise 147

SNP distances within Mab clusters (Figure 2A, Extended Data Figure 2). Regressing the SNP 148

distance between isolate pairs on the time between sample pairs yielded a mutation rate of 2.21 149

SNPs/year [1.06 – 3.37 95% CI], or 5.17x10-7 SNPs/site/year [2.48 x10-7 – 7.92x10-7 95% CI]. This 150

value is more comparable to previously reported molecular clock rate estimates within Mab 151

clusters4,9,12,13 than to those estimated in the long branches of the phylogeny (Figure 2C). 152


<!-- Page 8 -->


7

153

Simulated ancestries support mutation rate slow-down over population size effects as the major 154

driver of phylogenetic clustering. To test whether sampling from clades with low genetic diversity 155

is sufficient to explain the degree of clustering observed in the ML phylogeny, or whether changes 156

in the molecular clock rate are a better explanation for the observed phylognetic data, we 157

performed coalescent simulations of ancestries with one clustered subpopulation (A) and one 158

unclustered subpopulation (B). Under a range of effective population sizes (Ne) and mutation rates 159

(μ), we simulated ancestries through time with 1000 replicates per simulation. For each replicate 160

we assessed the degree of phylogenetic clustering by measuring dA/dB where di is the mean 161

pairwise SNP distance within subpopulation i. The total Ne (NeT), number of samples, and 162

sampling dates for subpopulations A and B were drawn from the true values for M. a. abscessus 163

DC 1 and from all “unclustered” isolates in our dataset, respectively (Figure 3A). We first tested 164

whether a smaller population size for the clustered subpopulation A (NeA) could explain the degree 165

of phylogenetic clustering observed. We estimated a range of realistic values for NeA using BEAST 166

by assuming a range of possible clock rates (Extended Data Table 4). These rates spanned a 167

published clock rate estimate for M. a. abscessus DC1 to a clock rate that is 50-fold higher, far 168

exceeding the upper 95% highest posterior density (HPD) interval for the published value13 Under 169

the the simulated conditions of equal mutation rates between subpopulation A and B, we only 170

observed phylogenetic clustering to the extent observed in the clinical isolate phylogeny in the 171

scenario where NeT >> NeA  (Figure 3B, Extended Data Figure 3). We next tested whether a change 172

in the mutation rate at the root of supopulation A could better explain the observed phylogenetic 173

structure in Mab. The simulated ancestries where NeA and NeB are fixed and the mutation rate 174

slowdown is between 10- and 20-fold recapitulated the observed phylognetic structure (Figure 175

3C). This result was robust to changes in NeA and NeT across the 95% HPD for each parameter 176

(Extended Data Figure 4). These results indicate that for person-to-person transmission to drive 177

phylogenetic clustering in Mab, the total Ne must be very large compared to the Ne of the clustered 178


<!-- Page 9 -->


8

subpopulation, an unlikely scenario given the observed genetic data and sampling times. By 179

contrast, a mutation rate change of 10- to 20- fold explains the degree of clustering observed in 180

Mab under more realistic population sizes given these data. 181

182

UvrD/Rep family helicases are enriched in DCs in M. a. abscessus. To identify genetic variants 183

under positive selection in Mab clusters, we searched for evidence of phylogenetic convergence 184

in the core genome of M. a. abscessus with regions of recombination excluded. Briefly, we 185

performed ancestral sequence reconstruction for the internal nodes of the subspecies tree and 186

counted the number of independent arisals of each SNP (Methods). Of the 65,202 SNPs identified 187

in M. a. abscessus, 34,813 (53.4%) of mutations occurred only once and were excluded. For the 188

remaining SNPs, we ranked each by its enrichment in DCs relative to other regions of the M. a. 189

abscessus tree (Figure 4A). The most significantly enriched variants in the M. a. abscessus DCs 190

included homologs of several known or putative virulence factors as well as a number of cluster- 191

enriched mutations in UvrD-like helicases MAB_1054, MAB_3515c, and MAB_3516c (Table 2, 192

*Figure 4A). While the function of these genes is not well characterized in M. abscessus, all three 193*

share homology with the UvrD/Rep family of helicases. This family of genes is involved in DNA 194

repair and has been associated with growth and persistence in vivo15,16. 195

196

Isolates in Mab DCs are associated with a lower spontaneous mutation rate. To test the 197

association between phylogenetic clustering and spontaneous mutation rate, we selected M. a. 198

abscessus and M. a. massiliense strains that were grouped within DCs or that were not present 199

in those clusters. Each of the strains present in the DCs has the derived (minor) allele at four sites 200

in the UvrD/Rep family genes MAB_1054, MAB_3515c, and MAB_3516c, and the strains outside 201

of DCs possess the ancestral (major) allele at those sites (Table 2, Figure 4A). The strains used 202

and their genotypes are described in Supplementary Data Tables 2 and 3. The spontaneous 203

mutation rate was estimated in all strains using a fluctuation assay17 adapted for use in M. 204


<!-- Page 10 -->


9

abscessus. The fluctuation assay counts cells gaining resistance to the antibiotic amikacin during 205

growth in culture without antibiotic. By normalizing the number of mutational events to the 206

population size of the culture, the fluctuation assay estimates the spontaneous mutation rate per 207

generation per the number of bases that can be mutated to confer resistance to amikacin. The 208

strains chosen display similar growth rates (Extended Data Figure 5) and very low baseline 209

resistance to amikacin (Extended Data Table 5) which allows them to be compared using a 210

fluctuation assay. Among M. a. abscessus strains, those present in DCs with the derived (minor) 211

allele at the four UvrD/Rep loci had lower spontaneous mutation rates than those with the 212

ancestral (major) allele (Figure 4C). A similar trend was observed in M. a. massiliense strains 213

(Figure 4D). Further, the average mutation rate was significantly lower in isolates present in DCs 214

across both subspecies (Figure 4E), consistent with the hypothesis that the emergence of dense 215

clustering may be driven in part by changes in mutation rate. 216

217

Discussion 218

In this study we have pooled a large global sample of Mab genome sequences and 219

examined evolutionary rates and positive selection with the goal of understanding the emergence 220

of Mab clusters. We present evidence supporting a slower evolutionary rate within DCs compared 221

to the long internal branches of the phylogeny and further data associating adaptive genetic 222

variation in DNA repair genes with the slower evolutionary rate. We posit that changes to the 223

mutation rate underlie the dense clustering in Mab, and that while other effects such as population 224

or transmission bottlenecks and sampling bias may contribute to the low genetic diversity within 225

clusters, they are not sufficient to explain the observed phylogenetic structure. 226

Previous studies have restricted molecular clock rate estimation to Mab clusters, most 227

likely because of the lack of temporal signal at the subspecies-level. By pruning the Mab tree 228

while preserving the majority of the subspecies diversity, we were able to measure a molecular 229

clock rate for Mab spanning the time scale from the common ancestor of the subspecies to the 230


<!-- Page 11 -->


10

present. Estimates of evolutionary rates are recognized to depend on the time scale of 231

measurement. In such examples, the clock rate usually decreases with increasing time depth18. 232

We observe the opposite effect where the clock rate increases with time depth. The pruned Mab 233

tree most likely reflects an evolutionary process taking place predominantly in environmental 234

reservoirs, in contrast to phylogenetic clusters where terminal branches reflect evolution within 235

the human lung environment. We also note that our measurement of within-host mutation rate in 236

Mab was independent of phylogenetic inference and the full temporal signal in our sample. 237

Nevertheless, the measured rate within-host was comparable to the clock rate measured 238

previously using coalescent analysis within clusters (Figure 2C). 239

The molecular clock rate is influenced by both the spontaneous mutation rate and the 240

generation time of an organism. Changes in generation time could result from physiological 241

constraints of the human lung environment, if for example, differences in nutrient availability 242

change the growth rate in the lung compared to those living in environmental reservoirs. 243

Generation times and spontaneous mutation rates can also be modified by genetic changes, for 244

example to DNA replication or repair machinery. The observation that some lineages have 245

adapted to the host environment 4 raises the possibility that genetic changes that underlie or 246

associate with this adaptation affect mutation rate, either directly by affecting DNA replication or 247

repair machinery, or indirectly by affecting the growth rate. Ruis et al. reported differences in 248

mutational signatures along internal branches of the subspecies phylogeny compared to internal 249

branches of DCs, supporting a change in the mutational process within some clades of the tree13. 250

We scanned the core genomes for variants enriched in the DCs in M. a. abscessus, the 251

subspecies for which we have the most WGS data and for which there are the highest number of 252

clusters. Notably, we observed several cluster-enriched mutations in UvrD-like helicases. UvrD is 253

a superfamily 1 helicase that is involved in DNA repair and is widely conserved in gram-negative 254

bacteria. UvrD1 in M. tuberculosis plays an important role both in nucleotide excision repair (NER) 255

and in pathogenesis and persistence because its DNA repair activity confers tolerance to reactive 256


<!-- Page 12 -->


11

oxygen intermediates (ROI) and reactive nitrogen intermediates (RNI)15. Mutations that promote 257

the activity of UvrD1 and its homologs are likely advantageous in the context of lung infection and 258

may have the additional consequence of decreasing the spontaneous mutation rate. We 259

additionally observed mutations in UvrD-like helicases occurring along the cluster-defining branch 260

of the large M. a. massiliense cluster, further supporting the role of the NER pathway in Mab 261

pathogenesis. 262

Our study has several limitations. Our dataset overrepresented clinical isolates from the 263

UK where routine whole genome sequencing is part of Mab surveillance. Oversampling of some 264

lineages and geographies may mean that we have not adequately captured the global population 265

structure and that we may have focused on large phylogenetic clusters because of their 266

geographic distribution and not because of their clinical significance. While our study argues 267

against transmission as the main driver of Mab dissemination and the emergence of DCs, we do 268

not examine the geographic distribution of Mab within clusters. It is possible that future work 269

considering this data can highlight mechanisms of parallel evolution that explain why clustered 270

Mab isolates are detected in distant geographic locations. While our results support a faster 271

molecular clock rate in the long internal branches of the phylogeny compared to clustered 272

lineages, we are unable to distinguish between rate differences due to the spontaneous mutation 273

rate from generation time effects. Differences in growth conditions across environments is difficult 274

to quantify as Mab is ubiquitous in both natural and built environments, but nutrient availability 275

likely differs greatly between natural reservoirs such as soil and water compared to man-made 276

reservoirs such as showerheads. A healthy lung supports relatively little bacterial growth, but 277

inflammation increases nutrient availability by promoting mucus production and vascular leakage 278

into the airway 19. Because there is little publicly available sequencing data from environmental 279

isolates, we were also unable to compare genotypes or mutation rates in environmental samples 280

compared to clinical isolates. Our analysis of variants associated with phylogenetic clustering is 281


<!-- Page 13 -->


12

also limited in its ability to identify true causal genotypes or those that are enriched in clusters due 282

to hitchhiking to other adaptive variants. 283

In summary, we present new evidence for changes in the molecular clock rate that 284

contribute to the dense phylogenetic clustering observed in Mab. These results argue against 285

person-to-person transmission as the primary driver of clustering in the Mab phylogeny. 286

Continuing genomic surveillance is needed to understand how Mab may be adapting to human 287

infection and to characterize the risk of transmission to at-risk patients. We argue further that the 288

phylogeographic structure of Mab is influenced by its complex ecological history as an emerging 289

facultative pathogen that should be considered carefully in future analysis of Mab genomic data. 290

Future work should extend these analyses by examining differences in mutation rates and 291

phenotypes between clinical isolates and environmental strains for evidence of host adaptation. 292

Methods 517

Data Sources and Description: WGS data were curated from published studies4,7,10,12,21–23 and 518

additional data were downloaded from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA). A search of 519

“abscessus” was conducted on October 4, 2019 using the filters “DNA” and “Illumina”. Sequences 520

were selected that had an associated date of collection with the year at minimum. Collection dates 521

were obtained either from the literature, SRA metadata table, or provided by the authors. A 522

summary of all samples used in this study is provided in Extended Data Table 1. Raw sequencing 523

reads were downloaded using the NCBI SRA toolkit24. 524

525

Quality control of Illumina reads: Reads were trimmed and filtered with trimmomatic25. To detect 526

contaminated samples, the mean GC content of the reads were compared to a modelled normal 527

distribution of GC content using fastqc26. If the sum of the deviations from the normal distribution 528

represented more than 30% of the reads, the sequencing run was excluded from further analysis. 529

Subspecies assignment and genome assembly: Multiple sequencing runs corresponding to one 530

biological sample were combined into one file. Reads were then assembled de novo using 531

SPAdes27. Assemblies were compared to a reference sequence for each of the three subspecies 532

(Supplementary Data Table 1) and a whole-genome based average nucleotide identity (gANI) 533

score was calculated using fastANI28. The resulting alignments were assigned to a subspecies 534


<!-- Page 23 -->


22

based on having gANI of at least 98% with exactly one reference strain. Isolates that did not have 535

at least 98% ANI with any reference strain were excluded. No isolates matched more than one 536

reference genome. After assigning isolates to a subspecies, reads were mapped to the 537

corresponding reference genome using BWA MEM29. After alignment, isolates with <80% 538

coverage of the reference genome at a depth of at least 20x or with missing data at >30% of sites 539

were excluded. 540

541

Variant calling and SNP filtering: Variants were called using Pilon30. We excluded ambiguous calls 542

as wells as indels and MNVs. We also excluded calls with low coverage using a minimum depth 543

of either 10% of the mean coverage, or 5, whichever was greater (default settings for Pilon – 544

mindepth). We used bcftools31 to exclude calls with mapping quality or base quality scores < 20. 545

546

Core genome inference: Unlike the professional mycobacterial pathogens M. tuberculosis or M. 547

leprae, which have small accessory genomes, M. abscessus has a large, open accessory 548

genome32. To define the core genome for phylogenetic analysis and to exclude loci that are highly 549

divergent from the reference sequence, we masked all loci for downstream analysis where read 550

depth was <20x in more than 5% of the isolates in our sample set. The remaining loci were 551

compared to an estimate of the core genome calculated by Roary33, and the two methods yielded 552

nearly identical results. We further excluded regions with average mapping quality scores or 553

average based quality scores <20. Finally, we used GenMap 34 to calculate mappability scores 554

across each reference genome as defined in reference35. We then calculated a mappability pileup 555

score for each base position as described in reference36 and excluded loci where the mappability 556

pileup score was <95% from downstream analysis. In total, we excluded 14.4%, 13.5%, and 557

15.1% of the M. a. abscessus, M. a. massiliense, and M. a. bolletii reference genome length, 558

respectively. 559

560


<!-- Page 24 -->


23

Phylogenetic tree inference: A full-length sequence alignment was created using a custom script, 561

masking loci excluded by our filtering criteria described above. Gubbins37 was used to predict and 562

mask regions of variation produced by recombination from the full-length alignment. A 563

recombination-free SNP alignment generated by Gubbins was then used to build a phylogeny for 564

each subspecies using IQ-TREE38, using the ModelFinder Plus (-mfp) option and 1000 bootstrap 565

replicates. Clusters were defined as previously described4 using a one-dimensional scanning 566

statistic to identify clades with a distribution of branch lengths that is shorter than the distribution 567

of branch lengths in the rest of the tree39. 568

569

Coalescent analysis: Temporal signal was assessed using root-to-tip regression. In both M. a. 570

abscessus and M. a. massiliense subspecies trees and all three major clusters, a slightly negative 571

slope was observed, indicated lack of temporal signal. We recognized that the high degree of 572

clustering and short time span over which the clustered isolates were sampled may confound the 573

genetic temporal signal. To address this, we pruned the trees down to taxa that preserved 95% 574

of the relative tree length (RTL) of the original trees using Treemmer40. A threshold of 95% 575

eliminated most of the dense clustering, but preserved the long branches of the original tree 576

(Figure 2B, Figure S2B). Using the pruned tree, we observed evidence of temporal signal in the 577

MAB subspecies using root-to-tip regression. We generated a SNP alignment including only the 578

taxa present in the pruned M. a. abscessus tree and used this as input for coalescent analysis 579

using BEAST214. ModelTest-NG41 was used to select the site model GTR+4. MegaX42 was used 580

to perform a maximum likelihood test to determine that a relaxed clock model is best suited for 581

our data. This choice was confirmed using the nested sampling algorithm to compare marginal 582

likelihoods for a strict v. relaxed clock model. We then used nested sampling to compare various 583

tree priors. We using Bayesian Evaluation of Temporal Signal (BETS) to confirm the presence of 584

temporal signal by comparing marginal likelihoods when the tip dates were used to those when 585

all samples were assumed to be isochronous (Extended Data Table 3). Based on marginal 586


<!-- Page 25 -->


24

likelihood values, we ran both a coalescent constant population model and a Bayesian skyline 587

coalescent model, assuming a relaxed clock and including the sampling dates for both models. 588

We used the ML phylogeny of the pruned dataset as a starting tree. For each model we ran two 589

independent chains for at least 100 million states to ensure convergence. 590

591

Phylogenetic dating: To attempt to date the full MAB phylogeny, we ran both coalescent constant 592

population and Bayesian skyline coalescent models assuming a relaxed clock without sampling 593

dates. We set the mean UCLD clock rate to the values estimated from our coalescent analysis of 594

the pruned tree. We ran each chain for at least 100 million states. 595

596

Estimation of mutation rate within-host: We identified 90 patients with two or more M. a. abscessus 597

isolates. Because coinfection with multiple M. abscessus clones is common in cystic fibrosis 598

patients, we first sought to exclude any isolate pairs that represented distinct clonal infections. 599

We selected a threshold of 20 SNPs by comparing the distribution of all possible within-host 600

isolate pairs to the distribution of pairwise SNP distances within Mab clusters. We further excluded 601

any isolates where >20% of the genome is predicted to be rearranged by recombination. For the 602

remaining isolate pairs we regressed the pairwise SNP distance between the first and last isolates 603

sampled from each patient on the time between the collection of each sample. The slope of the 604

regression line was used as an estimate of the number of SNPs accumulated over time. 605

606

Ancestry simulations: We used msprime43 to simulate ancestries to model two subpopulations: 607

(1) a “clustered” subpopulation (A) and (2) an “unclustered” subpopulation (B). We assumed a 608

constant population size and initially set the total effective population size (Ne) to 8000, the Ne 609

estimated in our coalescent analysis of the pruned Mab tree. We chose a range of realistic Ne for 610

subpopulation A, NeA by running a separate coalescent analysis of M. a. abscessus cluster 1 using 611

BEAST, assuming a constant population size, relaxed clock, and a range of UCLD clock rates 612


<!-- Page 26 -->


25

spanning 1.7x10-7 SNPs/site/year, as previously reported for this cluster by Ruis et al. (2021) to 613

8.5x10-6 SNPs/site/year, a value well above the 95% HPD interval for our estimate of the clock 614

rate in the pruned tree (Extended Data Table 4). We assumed the Ne of subpopulation B to be: 615

NeB = Netotal-NeA. The number of samples and sampling dates supplied to the model for 616

subpopulations A and B are drawn from the true values for Mab cluster 1 and from all 617

“unclustered” isolates in the tree, respectively. We assumed an initial mutation rate of 1x10-9 618

mutations/generation with a sequence length of 5Mb and a divergence time of 30,000 generations 619

between subpopulations A and B. We also assumed the nucleotide subsitution model estimated 620

using BEAST. 621

We first simulated a scenario where the mutation rate remains constant, varying NeA over 622

the range shown in Extended Data Table 4. For each simulated ancestry we overlaid mutation 623

events, supplying the model with a starting substitution rate of 1x10-9 mutations/generation, a 624

nucleotide substitution model estimated using BEAST, and a sequence length of 5Mb. We then 625

extracted the simulated genotypes and constructed a neighbor joining (NJ) tree. The NJ tree was 626

used to exclude any simulations where the two subpopulations did not exhibit reciprocal 627

monophyly.  We used the extracted genotypes to estimate the degree of clustering in each tree 628

by comparing the mean pairwise SNP distance in subpopulation A (dA) to the mean pairwise SNP 629

distance in subpopulation B (dB). For each simulated condition we performed 1000 replicates. To 630

simulate ancestries with a mutation rate change, we repeated the above procedure conservatively 631

assuming NeA = 718 (Extended Data Table 4). We modeled a per-generation mutation rate change 632

starting at the common ancestor node for subpopulation A and ranging from 1-fold (no change) 633

to 1/25-fold spanning a range of reasonable rate changes based on the range of clock rate 634

estimates observed in this study and reported in the literature (Figure 2B). For all simulated 635

conditions, we the simulation over a range of values for Netotal spanning the 95% HPD intervals for 636

the Ne estimates using the Treemmer tree under both the constant coalescent and coalescent 637

skyline tree priors. 638


<!-- Page 27 -->


26

639

Scan for variants enriched in host-adapted lineages: To search for variants associated with host- 640

adapted MAB lineages, we first inferred the number of independent arisals in the MAB phylogeny 641

for each SNP using SNPPar44. Briefly, SNPPar uses TreeTime to perform an ancestral sequence 642

reconstruction at each node, then infers mutation events arising on each branch of the tree. We 643

quantified the number of independent mutation events for each SNP. We considered only 644

mutation events where the derived call was the minor allele and the ancestral call was the major 645

allele. Because of the extreme phylogenetic clustering in Mab, we defined the major and minor 646

alleles using the pruned alignment generated by Treemmer.  For all homoplasic SNPs (occurring 647

two or more times independently in the tree), we used Fisher’s exact test to quantify the 648

enrichment of that variant within phylogenetic clusters. We conducted two separate analyses: a) 649

focusing on the three largest clusters in the M. a. abscessus tree (described in the main text), and 650

b) considering all clusters identified by this approach. In each case we obtained similar results. 651

For both analyses, full lists of variants ranked by their enrichment scores are provided in 652

Supplementary Data. We also used SNPPar to identify all mutation events occurring on the 653

branch ancestral to M. a. massiliense cluster 1. 654

655

M. abscessus culture: M. abscessus clinical isolates used for fluctuation assays were isolated 656

from patients in Taiwan and in Boston, MA, USA. All M. abscessus strains were cultured in 657

Middlebrook 7H9 broth (271310, BD Diagnostics, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) with 0.2% (v/v) 658

glycerol, 0.05% (v/v) Tween-80 (P1754, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and 10% (v/v) 659

OADC (90000-614, VWR, Radnor, PA, USA). Proliferation rates were determined by inoculating 660

5 mL media with 500,000 colony forming units (cfu), then measuring OD600 at 24 and 48 hours 661

post-inoculation. Proliferation rate was calculated as follows: proliferation rate in doublings per 662

day = log2(OD600 at 48 hours / OD600 at 24 hours). 663

664


<!-- Page 28 -->


27

Fluctuation Assay: Fluctuation assays were performed as described previously17 with adaptations 665

for M. abscessus. M. abscessus strains were grown to saturation, then diluted to an OD600 < 666

0.01 and grown overnight until cultures reached an OD600 = 0.6-0.8. These cultures were used 667

for fluctuation assays as well as determination of baseline amikacin sensitivity. Baseline amikacin 668

sensitivity was tested by spreading dilutions of 10 million, 100 million, or 1 billion cfu on agar 7H10 669

(262710, BD Diagnostics) + OADC (90000-614, VWR) + 300 µg/mL amikacin sulfate (A2324, 670

Sigma-Aldrich) plates. For fluctuation assays, 5000 cfu were plated in 1 mL media in each of 21 671

wells of a 24-well culture plate (10861-558, VWR), and initial cultures were plated for cfu on 7H10 672

+ OADC to confirm number of cells in initial culture. 24-well plates were incubated shaking at 150 673

rpm for 6 days at 37°C. 18 wells of each strain were plated onto 6-well plates containing 5 mL 674

7H10 agar + OADC + 300 µg/mL amikacin sulfate in each well. Amikacin was used as the 675

antibiotic selection for the assay because all tested strains had low baseline resistance (Extended 676

Data Table 5), which is required for the validity of the fluctuation assay. The remaining 3 wells 677

from each strain were diluted and plated on 7H10 + OADC plates to enumerate average final cfu. 678

Colonies on all agar plates were counted after 5 days incubation at 37°C. Mutation rate per 679

generation per total number of bases that can be mutated to confer amikacin resistance was 680

calculated using the Shinyflan application for the flan R package17 using the Maximum Likelihood 681

estimation method, assumption of unknown fitness effects of mutations, the Exponential (LD 682

model) distribution of mutant lifetime, and a Winsor parameter of 1024. One strain (BWH-E) was 683

excluded from analysis due to highly variable results across replicates (Figure S6B). 684
